cultivar: Seedling bushes and Tea Research Institute clones
processing: Fully oxidised orthodox black tea in the standard Ceylon pattern (wither, rotorvane and roller, fast oxidation, firing), sorted mostly into broken grades such as BOP and BOPF; the cool, dry air keeps the leaf small and the cup bright.
harvest_season: Year-round; the dry, cool weather of January and February, with cold nights, gives the best teas.
appearance_dry: Small, neat, dark brown broken leaf (BOP) or wiry orthodox leaf, with a touch of tip.
taste_profile: The lightest Ceylon: delicate, fragrant and brisk with cypress and citrus notes, a hint of mint and a clean, dry finish, often compared with Darjeeling.

brewing.notes: Go lighter than for other Ceylons: 90 °C, three minutes, no milk or only a drop.

vintage_note: Sold through the weekly Colombo auction by estate and grade (Pedro, whose teas also sell under the Mahagastotte mark, is a name to look for); the January and February invoices are the ones to seek out. Best within a year of manufacture. CTC and tea-bag grades are also made, but the orthodox BOP is the classic.
description:
Nuwara Eliya is the highest tea district in Sri Lanka, a plateau of lawns, old colonial hotels and tea at around 1,800 metres in the central hills. Its teas are the lightest and most delicate of all the Ceylons, pale, fragrant and brisk, and they are often compared with Darjeeling, though they are made in a very different way.

The leaf comes from seedling bushes and Tea Research Institute clones, and it is made orthodox style in the standard Ceylon pattern: a wither, rotorvane and roller, fast oxidation and firing, then sorting mostly into broken grades such as BOP and BOPF. The cool, dry air and slow growth at this altitude keep the leaf small and the cup bright.

Expect a very pale golden-orange liquor with a fragrant, slightly cypress-like aroma, notes of citrus and a hint of mint, a brisk, clean finish and little body. Brew it a touch cooler than other Ceylons, around 90 °C for three minutes, and skip the milk or use only a drop; it is a tea for drinking plain.

It is sold through the weekly Colombo auction by estate and grade, and January and February are the quality window: Pedro, whose teas also sell under the Mahagastotte mark, is a name to look for. Drink it within a year of manufacture. CTC and tea-bag grades are also made, but the orthodox BOP is the classic.

If you like it, the neighbouring Dimbula district makes a slightly fuller version of the same bright style.
sources_note: Sinhala native name is the place name plus 'tē' (tea); the Tamil form was not added. Estate names from memory.
history:
The town of Nuwara Eliya was founded by the explorer Samuel Baker in 1846 and grew into the cool hill retreat of British civil servants and planters in Ceylon. Tea came to the island's hills later: James Taylor planted tea elsewhere in Ceylon in 1867, and a coffee blight two years later pushed planters toward the new crop.

Little is documented about the first tea plantings in this district specifically. Pedro, one of its estates, is dated to 1885.

The best teas come in January and February, after the northeast monsoon, when the weather is dry and the nights are cold. Good lots still make news: in July 2022 a BOP from Pedro, sold under its Mahagastotte mark, reached a record Rs. 2,750 at the Colombo auction.
